title: Queues: Simulate Enqueue/Dequeue
oneLiner: First in, first out -- the mirror image of a stack's LIFO. Add to the back, remove from the front.
keyTakeaway: A queue is FIFO (first in, first out) -- the opposite discipline from a stack's LIFO (last in, first out). Real systems rely on this exact ordering guarantee constantly: task schedulers, message queues, and (later in this app) BFS's frontier all depend on "whoever got in line first gets served first," no matter what gets added after them.
explanation: A queue supports two moves: enqueue (add to the BACK) and dequeue (remove from the FRONT). That's the entire difference from a stack (see Stacks: Valid Parentheses), which adds and removes from the SAME end -- a queue's two ends are different, which is what gives it first-in-first-out order instead of last-in-first-out. This lesson encodes a sequence of operations as one array to keep it a single, plain function: each positive number means "enqueue this value," and a 0 means "dequeue -- remove and record whatever's at the front." Return the values that got dequeued, in the order they came out. Watch out for the classic mix-up: dequeuing from the wrong end (the back, like a stack would) instead of the front is the single most common bug when a queue gets implemented with an array or list that makes "remove from the end" the easy/fast operation to reach for out of habit.

visualizationSteps.message: Operations: [1, 2, 3, 0, 0]. Positive = enqueue (add to the back, right side). 0 = dequeue (remove from the front, left side). Empty queue to start.
enqueue(1) -- added to the back. Queue: [1] (front is the left end).
enqueue(2) -- added to the back. Queue: [1, 2] (front is the left end).
enqueue(3) -- added to the back. Queue: [1, 2, 3] (front is the left end).
dequeue() -- remove from the front: 1. Queue: [2, 3]. Dequeued so far: [1].
dequeue() -- remove from the front: 2. Queue: [3]. Dequeued so far: [1, 2].

complexity.note: Each of the n operations is O(1); the queue can grow to hold up to n items.
